utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you begin, there's one matter which I want to deal with, administrative matter, concerning the calendar which was handed in yesterday. If anybody wants to make a representation about that, they should do so as soon as possible. Secondly, I ought to make it clear that it cannot be a final calendar because it is subject to the requirements of the other cases before the Trial Chamber. But it's of a provisional nature, and you should work upon the basis of it. But as I say, it may be subject to change.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before the first witness is called, there is an issue about the level of protection, but possibly that could be dealt with in private session rather than troubling, at the moment, going into full closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 13 page 4194 redacted – private session 23 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: (Open session) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym for the next witness is pseudonym I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the duration of these proceedings, you will be known as Witness I. Will you please look at the piece of paper in front of you and confirm that that is your full name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness I, were you born in 1973, and did you, before the conflict, live in Gornja Rovna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at the plan on the ELMO to your right, but please don't dislodge it, is it the case that Gornja Rovna is a village in two parts, Rovna and Pezici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you an ABiH soldier and a member of the anti-tank BiH platoon deployed in the area of Pezici and Kruscica to fight against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You now live elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 26th/27th of January of 1993, was there an attack on the villages of Gornja Rovna and Kovacevac by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that time, were you in the village yourself, or were you elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, I was not in the village. I was in the area of the Travnik municipality, because at that time, we were defending ourselves from the Serbian Montenegrin aggressors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you learn of the attack, either the same day or subsequently, and from what people in the village told you about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I learned at the front line, near Travnik, that my village was attacked. I learned that through the radio. Then we left the front line in Travnik and came back to the village on the 2nd of February, 1993. That is when I learned what had happened in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time of the attack, were there any or many men of military age and position to defend the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Only about ten people remained in the village; that is, ten who would be able to defend it. The rest of them went to the front line in Travnik, Maglaj, and so on; Doboj. Most people were at the front lines facing the Serbian aggressors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of this attack, is it the case that no villager was killed but some houses and stables were burned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, several houses and barns were torched in the village, but there were no losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before that attack, had there been troop movements that you subsequently connected to the attack, troop movements by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Look, before this conflict, I absolutely did not believe that the HVO would attack us, and if I were now to look back at it, somebody perhaps would have told me that we would be attacked. For instance, on the way from Busovaca to my village, I had to pass several HVO checkpoints before I arrived in the village. They checked what was being brought into the village, and it wasn't just about the weapons. They even checked the flour you were bringing in, to see whether there were weapons hidden in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 15th of April of 1993, did you notice troop movements in the area of the Hotel Ribnjak, where there was a military base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, as early as April 15, it was the Serb army celebrating the day of the army, and there were -- the HVO was -- there were celebrations in the Motel Ribnjak, and then we saw them massing their troops, and we also saw some other people whom we had not seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage uniforms with the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that night, were you on the front lines at Kruscica, close to Vitez, when the attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: This was not a front line. This was just a guard. We were keeping guard around the village of Kruscica. In other words, our platoon was tasked with providing security for the people who lived in Kruscica. So I was in a part above Kruscica, called Stjene.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From there, did you have visibility over to your own village of Rovna and Pezici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to see the attack, the torching of houses and so on, as it occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. It was around 6.00 when you could see that houses and barns were on fire and that there was shooting going on around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About 6.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were captured with a colleague by soldiers in camouflage uniforms with HVO patches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to assist the Chamber at this stage, although I hope to cover the text in the summary, I'm going to be leading material that's more detailed from a witness statement, if that will help the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you taken to Zabrdze, near Kruscica -- and it may not be shown on our map -- with your hands tied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then to the village of Gornji Veceriska, which the Chamber can see to the top left of the screen, first to a house and then to a school building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Within the school, did HVO soldiers and civilians provoke you and beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a man nicknamed Cica, full name Maros Jozo, who used an automatic rifle to fire into the room where you were detained, above your heads, later putting the rifle against your head and asking you questions, threatening a burst of gunfire should he pull the trigger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following day, did soldiers threaten to liquidate you? Were you tied up again, blindfolded, taken outside and forced, despite the blindfolds, to get on to a tractor or its trailer, being sworn at in offensive terms, using the word "balija," and hit on the head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Taken by the tractor to another location, were you then forced into the trunk of a car, with a colleague of yours forced by rifle butts to join you in the trunk, you then being taken to an unknown destination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that destination, were you forced into a hole in the ground down which you climbed by an iron stepladder, the hole being about half a metre wide and five metres deep, having water, smelling as if a toilet, at the bottom of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the accommodation such that you and the one other person who was with you could only be there if one of you stood in the water and one of you stood on the ladder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you change positions, you and he, from time to time, until you were called out by soldiers, or a soldier, taken to a barracks some 500 metres away and into an office where you were interrogated by a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of what military group was that soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any particular part of the HVO, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. In my view, he was some security officer with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did there come a time in the interrogation when another soldier knocked on the door, asking if he could go to that funeral, and asking if you were a balija, being told by the interrogating officer that you were, and that the man could go freely, which led to that man beating you with boots to your body for some 15 minutes, and with fists, while you were kneeling against the wall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was your head then placed, under instruction, on a desk, and was your head hit on that desk several times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Being stopped when the leading officer said you had had enough and that there could be further beating later, the man who had conducted the beating telling you you would not leave the place alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The interrogating officer offered you a cigarette, which you accepted. He told you that you would be executed, gave you another cigarette, and had you taken away to a cell or place -- I beg your pardon -- back to the hole, where you met your colleague who had been with you in the hole before, that colleague telling you that he also had been beaten and that he also had been told he would be executed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You decided to stick together, insofar as you could, to fight it out. Did you spend that night, I think, in the hole in the ground, expecting to be executed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that the next day, when you were taken from the hole, you said goodbye to each other but were in fact not executed, of course, but taken to a bus bearing the Red Cross sign in order to deceive the BiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You asked where you were, and you were told that you were in Stojkovici, which is near to Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you please, if you can see it on the map that's on the overhead projector on your right, just move the map? Can you look at the map to your right, please, Witness I? If you move it so that we can find both Novi Travnik and Stojkovici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Stojkovici (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you move it so that it's in --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Stojkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And down a bit. There you are. Thank you very much. You were told that's where you were, but were you then told you were going to Kaonik camp, and were you indeed taken to Kaonik camp, being introduced to the commander, Aleksovski, wearing an HVO patch, who at that stage laughed and was provocative?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Taken to a cell, where you were not allowed to use the mattress, by now being in your fourth day of captivity, were you provided no food and you had only eaten about twice in the four days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't understand the language they are talking. I mean I do understand the language, but there's something wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there something wrong with the language or with the interpretation or with the quality of the sound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. Madam, you are not interpreting it rightly. I don't know if you're Ms. or Mrs. I don't know English enough. But there was a mattress. It's not true that we did not have some mattresses. And you seem to be speaking Croatian, and I'm not really conversant in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the solution is for me to go a little more slowly and to go for shorter sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as far as paragraph 6 is concerned, we heard yesterday evidence about this and we've heard evidence before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it can be taken relatively shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness I, in light of what you've heard the Presiding Judge say, we are going to deal much more summarily now with the remainder of your captivity. Were you beaten regularly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To such an extent that you, at one stage, gave up and preferred to die?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you taken, despite the beatings, on forced trench digging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again to such an extent that at one stage you asked to have your arms broken as the only method to avoid your being taken trench digging anymore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of some 26 people, who went trench digging, who never returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were efforts made not to beat you about the face, apparently for fear of discovery of mistreatment by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of the beatings and trench diggings, were you interrogated from time to time about your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know that it would be dangerous to acknowledge having come from Rovna or Pezici --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- because of the problems the HVO had had there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When people were killed trench digging, were other prisoners compelled to sign a statement saying that the deaths had been caused by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Eventually, were you registered with the Red Cross on the 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But even to the Red Cross, were you unable to tell the truth because of mistrust of the interpreter who was accompanying the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following Red Cross intervention, did Aleksovski take you to a dispensary one day because the Red Cross had said you had to receive some treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He took me to the outpatient clinic in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the treatment provide no relief for the condition you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. They refused to examine me when he told them where I had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you at one stage from the prison moved to a hangar with 60 prisoners whom you found to be in an awful condition of malnourishment and dirt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Later, were you obliged to do various other works for the HVO and their guards, including cutting their grass and planting their potatoes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear the sounds of other beatings throughout your time in the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see signs of the Red Cross being kept away by Aleksovski from cells that held somebody who may have been beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. I don't know if you are interpreting it wrongly. Will you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably my mistake on this occasion, trying to do things too quickly. There was one occasion when a Red Cross official asked about a cell numbered 4 which was padlocked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Red Cross didn't go into that cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who had been in that cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: There was an Arab who had been captured at Pucarevo or, rather, Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Eventually, did the commission of the ABiH and HVO attend at the prison to offer exchange, you saying that you would reject that, if they hadn't managed to effect your release already, and that you would wait for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were eventually exchanged in June of 1993? I beg your pardon. No. What was the date of your release?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: On the 19th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you even been able to inform your family, in the meantime, that you were still alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. Only after I came out, I learned that my village was under assault of blockade and that I could not get there, so that after I spent two months in Zenica, and then I came back to the village again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 8. During your time in the prison, first, did you see anything of a man called Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about a man called Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom was he mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, in the camp he was mentioned, a number of people ranging from the warden, Aleksovski, to those guards who were there in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did they refer to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, they referred to him as the boss, as the chief, as to someone who had the last say and the final say in the area. I heard someone refer to him as "Colonel" and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did Aleksovski speak of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I was once in the passage. I was sweeping the passage in the camp, and Aleksovski and Stipo Andrijesevic were standing in the passage. Stipo Andrijesevic was one of the camp guards. They were talking, and they were talking about what they had been doing during the Easter holidays spent with Kordic, and there was a corriga, a bullfighter, and how they knocked their eggs, and how Stipo Andrijesevic had the privilege of knocking his egg against Kordic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Aleksovski's conversation, could you tell anything about the order of superiority between Aleksovski and Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, I have to object. I think what Mr. Nice is seeking to have this witness do is offer his conclusions and speculations about what he overheard. I think he should be asked what he overheard, and the inferences to be drawn from that are matters for the Trial Chamber, not for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can ask the witness what he heard and what conclusions he drew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness I, what did you hear, and what conclusions did you draw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, the conclusion from that conversation between Aleksovski and Andrijasevic, I concluded that Kordic was the first man with regard to everything in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a particular conversation you heard about Mt. Busovaca, the corridor that leads to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: This was also at the time when I was in the camp down there at Kaonik. Something happened that I did not know much about at that time, but every two or three days I would be going to the barracks where the HVO intervention platoon was quartered. There were about 40 of them, and with a couple of other prisoners, I made their beds and cleaned -- swept those rooms they slept in. Then one day I went there and saw that they were gone, so we made the beds and left again. And I saw that they were fewer in number than before and that only six of them were there in the barracks. They seemed to be quite indignant about something. Judging by the way in which they talked, the language they used, one could assume that they had suffered some losses. So we were doing whatever we were ordered to do by them, and they talked, how they had suffered losses at the Busovacke staje, and cursing Kordic's mother, and Kordic, for pursuing erroneous policies, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Your Honour, I don't think the Chamber yet has aerial views of Kaonik before it in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we had some yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had them yesterday? I see. These ones, yes. In which case, then, I needn't trouble with plans, unless the plans that I've got are going to be more helpful. Have you seen them? I don't know if counsel have seen them yet, but if they're better, they're available. I don't need to trouble us with them otherwise. I would ask the chamber to look at 1869, please, if that could go on the ELMO. It's a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What does this show?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the interior of the Kaonik camp, the part in which I spent a major part of my time in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The cells, how big?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, they were about two by perhaps four metres. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the number of detainees. At first, when we were about 250 to 300, there would be 20 of us to a cell, and then -- it depended. Some would be released or taken away elsewhere, and then there would be less of us to a cell. The minimum number of men to a cell was four.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you allowed to eat outside your cells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, we ate outside the cells. There was a kind of table set up in the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it in that position that you were able to see the condition of other people when you heard about what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other plan or map to be put in, which is 2043.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does this show places that you were taken to for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shan't trouble with other maps, including the hand-drawn maps of the witness. If they haven't yet been distributed to Defence counsel, I'm certainly happy for them to see them as part of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following your release, did you visit or indeed return to your home village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. I said it already, I went back after two months. I crossed the mountains and reached my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a communications centre there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did that communications centre have equipment capable of picking up radio traffic in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was its range, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It was up to two kilometres, from what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you handed a tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Do you mean had it been -- was it handed over to me? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: When I went to that communications centre, there was a colleague of mine working there, or rather my neighbour, and he let me hear a tape telling about events during the attacks on my village between the 16th and 20th of April. And there was a conversation --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I just want you to tell us, please, the conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Right, yes. Well, this dialogue, that dialogue took place in codes: Puma 1, Puma 2. Puma 1 was -- no, Puma 2 was the one who was carrying out the orders of Puma 1, and the conversation was about attacking my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you hear on the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, it was about the attack on my village. In the end, Puma 1 ordered Puma 2 to attack the centre of the village. The latter one tried to, but did not -- really fell short of the plan, and he's reporting to Puma 1. And then Puma 1 orders him to attack the upper part of the village, and he also tries to do it, and again reports that he can't. Then Puma 1 orders him once again to conduct the attack, and the other one answers -- apparently he is quite irritated about the whole matter, and he says something about, "Kordic, fuck your mother, you come here and take it." I apologise for the language I use, but I'm just transmitting what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of Puma 2's rejection of the suggestion that he should do it, had he given any explanation of why he couldn't do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Puma 2 said to Puma 1, "We can't do anything here because every tree is a balija."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you recognise either of the voices on the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't able to recognise either of the two until I finally -- I mean, it finally dawned on me that one of the participants in the conversation was Kordic, and the other one, the person who was attacking the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know Kordic at that time? Did you know of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I did not know him in person, but I heard him and saw him in the media, because he was a public figure, a media figure -- the media figure in so-called Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you understand from the media transmissions was his role in either political or military life, or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: His role, as I saw it -- and again, I repeat that this is only my opinion -- I think that he had both a military and political role.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The result of what happened to you in the camps, and when trench digging and so on, have you been left with some medical conditions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I'm still suffering from some of the consequences of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You'll be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Witness, my name is Steve Sayers, and I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We speak a different language, and so you have to leave some time for interpretation. I'll try to make my questions clear. If they're not, you just tell me, and I'll make sure they are clear; is that all right? Now, as I understand it, Witness I, you've spent five days with the Prosecutor's investigators. November the 26th, 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave a statement, I believe, to the investigators of this Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- and I think that you signed it on the 11th of January, 1998. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was the product of four days of discussions with the investigators: the 26th of November, 1997, and the next day, the 27th of November, 1997; the 10th of January, 1998; and then the day that you signed the statement, January 11th, 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the interpreter in that interview was Emina Kaknjo; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then you signed another statement on the 5th of November, 1998, when you were asked by the investigator to come back to the subject and highlight certain topics. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That statement given on November the 5th, 1998, followed two days of testimony as Witness M in the Aleksovski case; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was two days later. This was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, I think we're --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I think that in fact I was a witness in the Aleksovski case in March of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right, March the 25th and the 24th, 1998. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, the testimony I do, but not the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But the point is that you gave another statement to the Prosecutors about six months after you testified -- six, eight months after you testified in the Aleksovski case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, I just refreshed this statement. That is, I highlighted the details that the investigators were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right, but that was at the investigator's request, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever given any testimony or made any statements to the state commission for gathering facts on war crimes in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, when you were meeting with the investigators for five days and immediately before you testified in the Aleksovski case, were you told that it was important to relate to them everything that you had seen, everything that you had heard, and that it was important not to miss out anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They expressed that to you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They told you it was important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It's hard to go back to all the details of events of six years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right, but the point I'm making here is that the investigators told that it was important to tell them everything that you knew, so that you could testify fully and make fully accurate statements; isn't that right? You have to say an oral response for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you understood that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just to go over -- if I may, I'll tell you the subjects that I'm going to be talking about, just so that everyone can follow it, and you can follow it too. Just some general questions to begin with. In 1993, when you were involved in hostilities in the spring and early summer of 1993, you were just 19 years old, weren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were a private in the Territorial Defence for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know what this "private" means.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, in your November the 5th, 1998, statement, here's what you said: "Before the attack on Kruscica and the surrounding villages, my ABiH platoon, to which I was allocated as private, was" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may very well be an American interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It may well be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: A soldier, a regular soldier. And when I said my platoon, that was my unit, where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand. We'll get into that. Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to mention that. I wouldn't like to reveal his identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I need to know the name of the commander, Witness I, if you would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness doesn't want to mention it, what's the relevance of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I think it's pretty relevant, Your Honour, because I think the evidence from this witness is going to show that the ABiH, which we have previously been informed was surprised on the morning of the 16th of April, was actually fully prepared for an attack in the area where this gentleman was deployed, and that he was given orders to prepare for such an attack. And I'd like to know the identity of the commander just so that we can follow the command structure up in our discovery efforts as this case goes on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear the examination about this, and we will decide whether it's necessary to have his name or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just stepping back one bit, Witness I, you were actually a member of the Muslim political party, the SDA, at this time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I was not a member, but I was -- you could say a supporter, because I voted for them. But I did not have a membership card then, and I do not have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, do you remember testifying at page 1.485 in the Aleksovski case, on March the 25th of last year, just a year ago, quote: "I was a member of the political party of Democratic Action in 1991"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, as I said, I don't know how you interpret it this way, a party member. I was not a party member as somebody who engaged in politics. I was not politically involved. In my view, you sort of ally yourself with a party or become its member if you vote for them. I made myself clear, by virtue of my voting for the Party of Democratic Action, I subscribed to this party, I became its member, but I was not politically involved, actively, in any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you're telling this Trial Chamber, a year after your Aleksovski testimony, that you weren't really a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a comment on the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, at the time that you say the HVO launched an offensive on the village of Gornja Rovna on January the 27th, you were, I believe you stated, in the town of Novi Travnik on the front line fighting against the Serb and the Montenegrin aggressors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were on the front lines there with your unit; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Which unit were you in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But what unit of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It was a detachment. It was called the Kaonik detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the MOS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you just tell the Trial Chamber what the MOS is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It stands for Muslim Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was your commander in the MOS, without naming him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know if you understand the distinction between the MOS and the Territorial Defence. These are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: So I'm not sure what your question is regarding MOS. I was never a member of MOS. I was a member of the Territorial Defence, and because the Territorial Defence was part of the BH army, I was a member of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just move on a little bit here. You say that the village of Gornja Rovna was defended on January the 27th by people who had hardly any weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But even though they had hardly any weapons and there were only ten men of military age in that village, according to your testimony today, your testimony is that nonetheless these ten individuals successfully repelled an HVO attack without any losses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then you did not get back to the area until February the 2nd, 1993, when you joined the front line against the Croats; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So the front lines had been established against the Croats by the TO, of which you were a member, as of February 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, had you heard, Witness I, about a massacre performed by members of the 7th Muslim Brigade in late January 1993 at the village of Dusina, involving many civilians who had been killed and a military commander there in the HVO by the name of Zvonimir or Zvonko Grabovac, who had been shot about a dozen times at close range with automatic weapons and had had his heart cut out from his body?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me break it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you know anything about Dusina, Witness I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Nothing specific. I hear it just now for the first time that a massacre occurred there, and Dusina is something that I'm actually not even very familiar with. I never went to that village. In my view, these questions, I don't understand their relevance. I'm not understanding what you're trying to prove.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, just for the Trial Chamber's information, there has been some reference to Dusina. I'm not sure if you're familiar with the geographical location of that village, so it might make some sense to have the witness identify the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have heard about it, and no doubt we're going to hear much more evidence about it. The witness says that he doesn't know anything about it, so I don't think it's going to take us very much more forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Had you heard about an incident on April the 14th, 1993, in which four HVO officers were kidnapped by members of the 7th Muslim Brigade outside the town of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you hear anything or see, on the television station from Zenica, Zetel, I think its name is, anything about the kidnapping of Commander Zivko Totic from the Jury Francetic Brigade of the HVO in Zenica on the evening of April the 15th, 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know what connection there is between Zenica and my village. If you saw the map, you would see very clearly where Zenica is and where Gornja Rovna and Pezici. What do I have to do with Zivko Totic and these higher officers? I absolutely do not know these people; nor do I have an interest in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand. But had you ever been informed by any of the media, by your colleagues in the army --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Listen, I do not wish to comment on something that I do not know, the capture of Zivko Totic. What I'm more interested in is what I personally saw and experienced. I hope that that is clear. I don't think that I'm here to comment on Zivko Totic and what happened to him and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just answer the question, if you would, Witness I. Had you heard about this incident? We'll see whether it's relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it. But, please, if I can have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You want a break?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take our break, 20 minutes. Ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers. I think we might move on from Zivko Totic, go on to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I will do precisely that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, sir, if I may, to the events of the evening of April the 15th and April the 16th in which you were involved. Now, your platoon, your anti-tank platoon, was employed in Kruscica and the surrounding villages on the front line with the HVO, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer, or should I perhaps -- we should clarify something here. In Kruscica, for instance, there were no front lines there, because the conflict with the HVO had not started yet. There were a kind of local guards, just for security's sake, because Kruscica and Pezici are very close to one another, and one knew that if Pezici fell, Kruscica would fall too, so that certain measures were taken to forestall the situation, as in Kovacevac and other places. In other words, there were some guards there simply to take care of the people living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation, and coming back to my question, you were actually located on the front line with the HVO from the evening of April the 15th to April the 16th, 1993, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, not on the line. You seem to be confusing these two words. "Line" is one thing, and "guards" is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let me -- I'm not using my words, I'm using your words, actually. Let me just read to you a line from your witness statement that you signed on the 11th of January, 1998: "On the 16th of April, 1993, I was on the front line at Kruscica near Vitez. We were guarding the villages because we felt there was something in the air." You said that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, we thought -- can you grasp that? Because we thought those were not front lines; we were not dug in or anything of the sort. Those were just guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in the evening of April the 15th, you observed heavy troop movements on the part of the HVO and regarded it as absolutely obvious that they were preparing for a fight, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed that's what happened: There was a fight, wasn't there, after you had observed these troop movements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning of the 16th, they attacked us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in fact your level of alertness was increased by your unit commander, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. We already knew what had happened in Kovacevac and Pezici, so -- we already knew these things, but I'm telling you that Kruscica depended on Pezici and Pezici depended on Kruscica. If one fell, then the other one would fall, too. That was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Before the hostilities actually started, you and the other troops in your unit were sent to guard a hill called Stjene against the expected HVO assault; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. It's a hill nearby, near Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When the fighting started, you and a colleague by the name of Mustafa Hodzic were captured, and that was after about five hours of heavy fighting, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: We were not fighting there. There was no fighting there. We were surrounded by the HVO unit, and we were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Kruscica, I believe, sir, was a TO headquarters whose commander was Safet Sivro; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Kruscica, the TO headquarters in Kruscica, was just a short distance away from where you were sent to guard the hill called Stjene; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, about a kilometre, kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The TO actually had other headquarters at the villages of Preocica and Poculica, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, over there on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Those are TO headquarters on both sides of the main spinal road that leads from Busovaca, up through Kaonik, and takes a left and goes through Vitez on its way to Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In one of the diagrams that was attached to your earlier statements, you drew or identified a location where HVO artillery pieces were stored behind prisoners' quarters at Kaonik, and it was your view that that had occurred because the HVO knew that the BiH army would not shell the prison facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's no doubt at all on our position that the ABiH actually had artillery with which to shell that facility at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Listen, the Kaonik camp and all the adjacent places controlled by the BH army, the range of those pieces were relatively small, they could hardly threaten those places, and there was very little ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The point I'm trying to make is that the BH army actually did have artillery pieces in its inventory of weapons that it had at its disposal for either offensive or defensive purposes; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Why, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to another subject, if I may, the testimony that you gave concerning Mr. Aleksovski and the Red Cross. It's true, is it not, that during your two months of captivity at the Kaonik camp, that there were numerous visits from the international committee for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, every 15 days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, and in fact you met with one of the Red Cross representatives, a lady by the name of Beatrice is that correct, or Biatriche?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, when she met you for registration purposes, she actually asked to see you alone, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, not alone. There could have been about 20 of us when the Red Cross registered us when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. But she did ask -- maybe I'm confused on that, but at some point she did ask to see you alone, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, that is not true. She asked me what had happened to me, because I had a scar over my left eye, and she asked me about it. I didn't want to tell her the truth because I knew that I would be beaten again after that, so I said I had been digging and hit myself with the shovel, and asked them to take me to a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, let me just read you a portion from the statement that you gave on the 11th of January, 1998, regarding a meeting with this lady that I've identified and Mr. Aleksovski. "We sat around the table in the hallway where we usually had our meals. I heard that she asked Aleksovski to leave because she wanted to speak with us in private. Aleksovski left, and the procedure with the registration started." Right? So she did speak with you without the presence of HVO troops or without the presence of Mr. Aleksovski; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, after she registered us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You told her, sir, that you wanted to see a doctor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I wanted to be treated, because I was in a horrible state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Later that day, Mr. Aleksovski drove you and two other people from the Kaonik camp in his own personal car to the outpatient clinic in Busovaca, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, Counsel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Not that same day. It was the next time when Mrs. Beatrice came, only that when she came the second time, when I asked again to ask to see a doctor, and that is when it was done. So it could have been a fortnight later, but not that first time, not -- that first time, I had no medical help at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember telling the investigators, sir, on January the 11th, 1998, the following: "She," Beatrice, "told the commander, Aleksovski, that I should see the --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you please slow down? The interpreters don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: "She told the commander, Aleksovski, that I should see the doctor. He did not take me there immediately but in the evening"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, but that was when she came the second time. I again asked to see a doctor, and then she told Aleksovski that I should go to a doctor. Then in the evening, he took me and two others. He drove by a car to the outpatient clinic in Busovaca, and I was not extended help there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, the point is, though, that Mr. Aleksovski was told that you should see a doctor, and he took you to see a doctor that same day in his own car, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we've got the point here. There's no need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you were taken to see the doctor, you gave them a false name, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave them a false rank, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I didn't have any rank, if you mean a military rank. I had no rank. I went to see a doctor or, rather, Aleksovski drove me to a doctor. I was the last one of the three to enter the surgery, and they asked my name. I lied about that. Then Aleksovski said that I should give them my true name and where I came from. Then I said where I came from and who I was, and then finally they told me if I get out alive of this, then to go to doctors for treatment to Zenica because they were not going to treat me there. I was given some three pills --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [Obscured by interpretation] the question. You gave them false information about your rank, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he didn't have a rank, so let's go on. Anyway, I'm not sure it's going to assist us very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the basis for the conclusions that you reached regarding the relationship between Mr. Kordic and Mr. Andrijasevic. Do I understand that the sole basis for your conclusions in that regard were the snippet of conversation that you overheard between Mr. -- (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Aleksovski and Mr. Andrijasevic while you were cleaning in the hallway of the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that there were three or four hundred people at that Easter party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I haven't the slightest, how many of them there were. I never heard the figure, three hundred, four hundred, I mean, and I never mentioned any figure. I never said there were 300 or 400 people at that party. I simply don't have that kind of information. The only information I have is what I heard during the dialogue between Aleksovski and Andrijasevic, and that was about all those Easter eggs and how Andrijasevic was knocking his egg against Kordic's egg, and that's about it. That was the dialogue. They really enjoyed it, and they said that they had had a great time and things like that. I really don't know what else you want to know. I mean what else could I conclude but that they were at Kordic's, that they went to his place? Where would they then go, whether it was in Busovaca, whether in Vitez or where, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't know where this Easter party was held, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You really don't know anything about it, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness has given his evidence about it. It's what he overheard somebody say, and that is the extent of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Just a few clean-up questions on this particular subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You testified, I believe, that you've never spoken to Mr. Kordic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've never met him, have you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Never. Personally, no, never, except this is the first time I see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You never saw him during the two months that you spent at the Kaonik facility, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He never visited there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One final question. You would concede, would you not, that you don't know what the ranks or insignia or military structure of the HVO was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know. I know just that Mr. Kordic was referred to as a colonel. But what other ranks and all those things, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on to the final part of my questions, and that concerns the audiotaped conversation about which you gave testimony to the Trial Chamber. Just a few questions on this. The first is this: Where is the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The tape was a conversation between two people that lasted about five minutes, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your testimony is that five-minute conversation involved three separate attacks on Gornja Rovna or somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Not Gornja Rovna. Pezici, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was the name "Gornja Rovna" mentioned once in that taped conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The location of this alleged attack wasn't mentioned anywhere in the conversation, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The location was mentioned. It said "attack that wood" or "attack the upper part", and that was a reference to that part of our place which is in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How did you [indiscernible]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't but know. I mean these communications devices which recorded a conversation had very short range, not more than two kilometres. That was the range. Anything that happened during that conversation or, rather, what they talked about, all the instructions for the attack, all this was taking place in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's see. The first description of this conversation that you gave occurred over a four-day period in November 1997 and January of 1998, and that's about four or five years after this five-minute audiotape that you heard; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Had you ever heard the tape after you first heard it on August the 19th, 1993, according to your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: People still talk about that in my village and how these things happened and all that. Everybody knows about it, except that we -- or I mean I never thought that all this would happen. I never thought that I would be here talking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you first told the Prosecutor that this conversation was between two HVO officers; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did they identify themselves as officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. They were using secret names, Puma 1 and Puma 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you don't know whether these people were officers or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: How do I know who was what? Would you know if somebody is Puma 1 or not? Would you know whether he was an officer or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the first version of this conversation that you related to the investigators five years ago was that instead of ordering an attack on the centre, there was actually an order to attack the upper part first, not the centre. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I didn't understand the way you put your question. Could you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fine. The first time that you told the story to the investigators, you told the investigators that the order to attack was to attack the upper part first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: To attack -- to attack the upper part of the village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So the testimony that you just gave, that the attack was to be on the centre first and then, if that failed, or when that failed, to attack the upper part, and when that failed, to go and attack the lower part, that's actually not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I really don't know what you're driving at. First the order was to attack the upper part of the village, on the cassette. First the upper part of the village; then, if that would be impossible, then the lower part or the centre. But all in all, I mean, there were several attacks on the village between the 16th and the 20th of April, and there was a five-minute conversation, and it's just too short. It was way too short to record all these attacks and to do that; simply -- the first instruction, for instance, on that cassette, was to attack the upper part of the village, and if that failed, then they should attack the centre; and if they couldn't take the centre, then they were ordered again to attack the upper part of the village. And after that, after that failed, then things that I already described happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Well, isn't it true that when you were asked to or invited back by the investigators to highlight certain topics of your testimony, you told them, in November of last year, the following: "Puma 1 was ordering Puma 2 to attack the centre. After some minutes, Puma 2 answered that it was impossible. Then Puma 1 ordered to attack the part above."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: To attack the part above, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, what was the order? To attack the centre first, or the part above, or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has dealt with that. He has told us what he said the order was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would concede that the tape quality was pretty bad, Witness I, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You didn't recognise the voice, did you, when you heard the tape? Either of the voices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. I would never have known who they were had Puma 2 not cursed Puma 1 and used his name, because that is when he mentioned Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But you, frankly, sir, had no idea whether Puma 2 was talking to Puma 1 or Mr. Kordic, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Truth to tell, whether Puma 1 was Kordic, according to the cassette, yes, he was. But whether it really was he or not, you have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You just don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I was clear, I think. Listening to that tape, I concluded that it was Kordic. Whether that was he indeed, you have to ask him. Can't you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I know that that was your conclusion, but you don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, let's go on from this point. We have the evidence on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm pretty close to the end here, Your Honour. Just a few final cleanup matters, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You said that this conversation had supposedly been recorded by the ABiH in Gornja Rovna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At a communications facility that the ABiH had stationed in Gornja Rovna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you explained that this tape was supposedly made so that it could be compared with the way the HVO tried to attack the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That tape was made in the attack on my village, on Pezici, between the 16th and 20th of April. That is when the tape was made. That is when it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, in your highlighting of certain things to the Prosecutor about seven months ago, you said, "It was recorded in the BiHA communication centre of Gornja Rovna while the attack was going on so that it could be compared to the way the HVO tried to attack the village." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: To compare, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the testimony that you have given regarding the conversations by the HVO guards or the references by the HVO guards, supposedly, to Mr. Kordic as the chief or the boss or whatever, and the curses that were supposedly uttered against Mr. Kordic, that's the first time that you have ever told this story, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's not in any of your previous statements, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: What's that got to do with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's not in the two days of testimony that you gave in the Aleksovski case concerning the conditions of your confinement and the circumstances of your confinement in Kaonik, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: What's Aleksovski got to do with -- what's the Aleksovski case got to do with curses addressed to Kordic? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The point I'm making is that you've never previously given that testimony in Aleksovski or to the investigators in any of the numerous conversations that you've had with them; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: If we are talking about the Kordic case and when they asked me to give them the information that I had, or rather to tell them things that I had heard in the camp, those were the particulars I knew, that they were conversations between Aleksovski and -- with Aleksovski and Andrijasevic, that those from the intervention platoon of the HVO cursed him, and they were mentioning him. That is what I knew. I don't know what else you want to know. Apart from that, I don't know. Can you remember what you did six years ago? You know, I went through something horrible in my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness I, I know this is difficult, but please don't argue with counsel, and we'll finish more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The final question I have for this witness, Your Honour, is:

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who General Milivoj Petkovic is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No further questions, unless the Trial Chamber has any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the question I have is this: Is it disputed that Mr. Kordic was Puma 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Our position is that that is fiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the witness has made that up?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You had better put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you actually made up that conversation, that there never was an audiotape, Mr. I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I never made it up. I repeated what I had heard, and I have no intention of making anything up, nor am I interested in that sort of thing. Do you understand it? It was crystal clear what was going on. If it is not clear to you, then we can talk, and I'll try to clear the matters up for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honours. In the brief dated the 3rd of May, 1999, Prosecutor's witness, 247, the witness is mentioned at point 247 on page 18, and the first group of witnesses who had allegedly had a direct contact with any of the accused. Along with his name are stated the counts of the indictment to which the testimony refers. But we've just heard the testimony, and thanks to what is stated, that witness had nothing to do with the counts that the accused, my defendant, Mario Cerkez, is charged with, so we have no questions in this cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about membership or support of the political party, the SDA, and two words in English translated to your own language used were, first, "supporter"; second, "member." Can you explain, if it's possible, whether those two words have distinct and different meanings at the time that we are speaking of? If so, what was a supporter, what was a member, of a political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, a member is a member. For somebody to be a member of a party, he would have to have a membership card and be included in the work of that party. As a sympathiser, or supporter, that is -- well, it's something that you have sympathy for, something that you have opted for, for a political party which presents its views and positions, whether you vote for it or not. That is what a supporter means, whereas a member, I was never a member, nor did I remain a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Red Cross staff member, Beatrice, when she visited, did she visit alone, or did she need the services of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. She needed the services of an interpreter, and she was always accompanied by an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When Aleksovski left the room, did the interpreter remain behind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't trust one of the interpreters that would come with him, because the first time -- and this proved to be true, because when we asked for medical assistance the first time, Beatrice was there, and so was the interpreter, and we were alone, but we didn't get it -- get her, and this had to be conveyed back to Aleksovski. The second time, she came with another interpreter; we were given medical treatment, so the message was conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why did you not give completely accurate details, then, to the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Because I didn't dare. I knew that if I said something, they would beat me in the camp and would make me go digging or doing something that was against my will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: And so I'd be abused after that, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Beatrice give Aleksovski advice as to the future treatment that you should receive, and any advice about trench digging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, Beatrice told Aleksovski -- and we listened to the interpretation of what she said -- she told him that we were not to go digging, as human shields, and not to engage in any strenuous physical labour, that we were not to be abused, we were not to be left to go hungry or without clothing, which is what we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was her advice to Aleksovski followed, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, never. To the last day of my stay in the camp, I went on digging, and I went on doing all the jobs that the HVO soldiers had ordered me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The trip to Zenica for medical treatment, as you explained, and indeed as is set out in your statement at page 10, was on the second visit of Beatrice to the camp. Following such treatment as you received, what, if anything, did Aleksovski say about your getting treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, when I returned from Busovaca, I didn't receive any medical treatment. But when they learnt where I came from and who I was, he gave me some three pills. I had no idea what the pills were for. And on my return from Busovaca, he said, "Well, don't say that we didn't send you off to a doctor and that you were not given medical care and attention." But of course the medical treatment was nonexistent. They told me, at the outpatient department at Busovaca, "If you have come out alive, go and get treatment in Zenica. We're not going to treat you here."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The tape, you were asked how did you know that this related to events in your village; by whom were you given the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: My neighbour gave me my tape, my colleague -- how can I put it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just "Yes" or "No," did he tell you the circumstances in which he got the tape, where he had got the tape from when it was made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: He took the tape because he worked in a communications facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he tell you when the tape had been made and the circumstances of its being made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: He said that it was between the 16th and 20th of April, when my village found itself under attack by the HVO. That was when it was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How consistent or otherwise was what you heard on the tape with what you knew, both from what you'd been able to see from your position further to the west and with what you had heard from villagers who had been there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Everything on the cassette, you can compare the cassette, and you can superimpose it in the field and compare.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you made efforts to obtain that cassette since? "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of whom have you made efforts, or to whom have you made requests?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That same man, the same man that I listened to the cassette with for the first time. I contacted him and asked him where the cassette was, whether he still had it, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to get the cassette from him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
