utterances.text: One of your statements says that the tape was made so that it can be compared; it may be a language matter, but what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, the cassette was made, as I say, when the attack was launched on my village between the 16th and 20th of April. And the cassette clearly -- you can clearly compare what had happened and compare it to the tales of the population, my brother or father who were up there at the time, what they said. You could clearly compare the cassette with what had happened in the village and what people said had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about accounts you have given today of things said at the camp about Kordic and Aleksovski -- and I propose simply to lead with this, or I can put the detail in if my friends would prefer -- did you in both statements make reference to Aleksovski and his contacts with Kordic and what was said about Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, in both statements, I think I did mention that, that they had the Easter festivities and that they had this corrida of eggs, this egg-knocking, and the discussion between Andrijasevic and the other, and Kordic was mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those are the only questions I ask of this witness in re-examination. The only point that I'm invited to consider -- and I think, especially as we are now not under pressure of time, it's worth considering -- is whether the Chamber would be assisted by one slightly better map of Kaonik, because otherwise I might forget it for later, and if this witness can deal with it, then we've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that other witnesses coming along will deal with it, and we have a large version of it on the board over there. You can see it in the corner of the court. I'm not suggesting we get it out now, but the Court can see it; it can be used for pointing to. It's number 1870. And if we put it on the ELMO, please, facing north, that will fit with my general practice. Usher, if you could put it round so that it faces north? There's a "North" pointer. It doesn't have to be square on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does this show Kaonik camp, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: This photo shows an area, but -- a particular area. As to the camp, well, it's here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Use the pointer by the glass on your table. Use the pointer with the glass on your table. Without moving your head too much, because it's -- keeping your head in the same position, just point roughly where it is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: (Indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Tribunal will recall from yesterday's photograph the distinctive shape of the road or track that leads from the right of the point marked by the witness to join the road system, and that's one way one can connect the camp up. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness I, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to go back into open session. (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would have been more satisfactory had I had another half an hour's evidence that I could have led this morning, but alas, I don't. Equally, I don't have the embarrassment of having to send witnesses back, their time having been completely wasted. Can I raise or mention just a couple of points, some matters of detail which the time we have enables us to deal with? Some considerable time ago -- it feels that; it probably wasn't such a very long time ago -- through the witness Mr. Ahmic, a number of photographs were produced, and their exhibit number was 1593A. The Chamber will recall the speed at which I went through them, and I went through them perhaps too quickly as to one, number 33, because I was told by one of the court interpreters afterwards that what was read out by me, and indeed what appears on the index as to what was written on the wall, was incorrect. Now, it may seem a small point, but it may have some significance. If the usher could just put 33 on the ELMO for us, and if the chamber would be good enough to look to its index, can I ask the interpreters, if they can read it, and it's legible, to tell us what religious festival is spoken of on the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Easter. It says, "Happy Easter."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber will see that the index, therefore, is wrong, and although it may seem a small point, in view of the timing of events in April, it may not be wholly insignificant. I'm grateful both to the interpreters for dealing with that today and also for having taken the trouble to alert me to what I had got wrong or what had been got wrong earlier and I had repeated. The second point, the attitude of the Defence, as expressed in correspondence and argument, about the taking of witness statements has radically changed from an all-out suggestion that they are taken in bad faith and slanted to an open and complete acknowledgment of the reverse. As you know, I have intended to make available the investigator and indeed, if necessary, the lawyer who took the statement, the second statement from Dr. Mujezinovic. It may be that the changing approach of the Defence means that that is no longer required of them. If it is, then the witnesses will, of course, be tendered in a way which the Chamber would probably regard as conventional if such an attack is to be made. But I would be grateful to know from the Defence if they now wish to have the opportunity of cross-examining, in particular, the investigator who took the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, can you deal with that now or will you indicate in due course?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think I need a few minutes to mull that over, and perhaps it would be better if it were dealt with in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can send a message through the usual channels when you've decided, but if you would attend to that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The timetable for following witnesses has been necessarily affected by the new sitting dates and, to some degree, by the discussion we've had about witnesses. I shall be in a position to tell my friends, I hope by the end of the morning, precisely the names of witnesses I intend to call, although I think they will all be within the listed 60. For the Chamber's assistance, where we have three afternoons followed by a Friday, Saturday, and Sunday before another sitting, I'm necessarily going to be somewhat conservative in the number of witnesses I call here, because it wouldn't be desirable to keep people over that long weekend. I suspect that we will opt for some of the witnesses who were stood down this week, which are short witnesses in theory, capable of providing direct evidence about one or other defendant, and it may be it will be one witness per afternoon. There is the risk that the afternoons will be shorter than would be normal, depending on the cross-examination, but I hope that's an acceptable compromise, given the difficulty about interrupted sittings. We will do our best to keep those afternoons full of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it seems a sensible course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thereafter, we will probably provide a change of, as it were, diet. We'll deal with the outstanding evidence, if he's available, of Mr. McLeod and probably, I think, follow with a journalist or a witness who can provide an overview, because it seems to us that this is likely -- this general development of the case with all types of witnesses is likely to be more helpful than just having one category at a time. The expert reports, which I hope to have served next week, although one of them is long, I will have them marked, if this is helpful, by tab or by sidelines, with concluding paragraphs, that it may be are all that the Chamber need preread until it knows what is in issue as between the parties. Finally, and I only feel it's perhaps helpful to mention this in light of the very helpful schedule that the Chamber has provided, it might be that any trip that the Chamber wanted to conduct would be something that could happen relatively soon. That is to say, by now the Chamber is probably beginning to get a sufficient feel for the area overall as to know the places it would or might want to see, and of course parties on one side and the other could also point out what matters might be of value. I mention that because, of course, if there is to be a trip, it would probably have to be within the timetable that's been identified so far and, for reasons of weather, not after October, I would have guessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, there are security considerations to be taken account of before any visit can be made. If you wish the matter to be considered formally, perhaps you could briefly put the proposal into writing and it can then be considered here and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll do that, because I think it is our view that this would help. It's very difficult, I suspect, for even those who may have experience of maps in other areas fully to understand the scale on the ground of this territory, how intimate one place is to another and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would then put the matter into writing, outlining the places that you think it appropriate for the Trial Chamber to go to, the Defence can then respond, and perhaps this could be dealt with as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to go into great length about it, but the places must be clear so that a decision can be made about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you wanted to raise something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A very short matter, Your Honour. It concerns the motion to exclude four witnesses that was heard, I believe, on June the 3rd of 1999, and I wanted to clear up a factual inaccuracy that is contained on page 3221 and 3222. It concerns receipts of statements from two witnesses that were not among the four involved, and I had informed the Trial Chamber that we had received, on the night before, the evening before June the 2nd, two statements from a gentleman by the name of Hajrudin Indic and a gentleman by the name of David Pinter, and I informed the Trial Chamber that these gentlemen had not been listed on the witness lists. It's since been suggested that that was a misrepresentation. To me, that was a peripheral matter, because we were actually just using those by way of example. We did receive those statements for the first time on June the 2nd, 1999, obviously. With respect to the first one, Mr. Hajrudin Indic, "Indic" is apparently the gentleman's surname, and he was never listed by that name in the witness lists. He was actually listed as variously Mr. Haludine or Mr. Hajrudin rather than Mr. Indic. He was actually also identified as Mr. Indic, so I'm afraid we weren't able to determine that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [indiscernible] in fact been listed on the witness list, and I wanted to bring that to the Trial Chamber's attention. With respect to the second gentleman, David Pinter, he actually did appear on the witness list and I just made a mistake on that, and I apologise for it. I just wanted to bring that to the Trial Court's attention to clear up any inaccuracy that's contained in the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just make a comment on that? It was a matter of grave concern to us that names which were quite clearly on the list and which had been identified as witnesses to be called were then subject to the suggestion that statements were served outside time, and it simply wasn't accurate. Of course, the reference was made in the course of the recurring suggestion that there has been service of material outside deadlines, which is simply not true, and in the course of an important legal argument one name appeared on the list in exactly the same form, "David Pinter", and the other name appeared simply by the reverse, "Smith John" as opposed to "John Smith", it being said by the Defence that these names didn't appear anywhere on the list. What we have done, because of this recurring and unfortunate approach by the Defence, is we have prepared an authoritative, complete list of the production of documents. It's been filed yesterday. It is clear, and it is to be hoped that these errors don't happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may respond very briefly, Your Honour. The point that was being made was that these statements had been delivered to us for the first time on June the 2nd, way beyond the May the 17th deadline that this Trial Chamber had imposed for the delivery of statements. I might add, Your Honour, that those statements continue to be delivered. In fact, we have another receipt here, admittedly for people who have been identified, but for the first time in English, the final statements for the first time in English, June the 14th. So I don't think that it's a significant matter. I was using those two names by way of illustration, but the point to be made was that we received those witnesses' statements for the first time on June the 2nd, 1999, and that is accurate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to -- Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, just two words from me. Our dear colleague Mr. Nice mentioned a plan for the witnesses after the intermission that we're going to have lasting several days. He talked about many witnesses, and we are informed -- we have been informed of the list, but the problem is that always the first three or four, because we don't know which witnesses will be called until the very last. So could he please inform us, of those 40, 50 or 60, to give us the first seven witnesses? He doesn't have to proceed in that particular order, but we would like to know the group of witnesses to be called in the first couple of days. It doesn't matter whether on the first, second or third day, but we should like to prepare. As we are travelling, my office is here at the moment, so I take the documents I need for the first ten witnesses, and when I go back to my office in Croatia, I get a fax saying it's not those particular ten but other ten witnesses. So those are the technical problems that occur. Of course, it can be solved, but it does mean losing a lot of time and concentrating on things that are not essential. So we don't insist that the seven names he gives us should proceed in that order, but we would like to have the seven, regardless of the order, the witnesses called in the first three or four days, and that would facilitate our work greatly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My colleagues have been working on the list this very morning, and I think a fax is being prepared at this very moment, or pretty well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, and if the Trial Chamber could have a copy of it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to deal next with a ruling arising from the discussion yesterday concerning the dossier of evidence. There is a need to clarify the issues in this case, in the judgement of the Trial Chamber, and to determine what issues are in dispute and what are not. The purpose for doing this is in order to secure, as we must, a fair and expeditious trial, "fair" meaning fair, of course, to both sides. The dossier which the Prosecution have produced can be of assistance in this regard and can be of assistance in clarifying the issues relating to the attacks on the various villages. We do not propose at the moment to rule on whether the dossier or any part of it should be admitted, but we do think it not unreasonable, in a trial of this size and complexity, that the Defence should play its part in clarifying the issues for the parties and for the Trial Chamber. Accordingly, we propose to make use of our powers under Rules 89(C) and 90(G) and make an order generally in this way: First, we formally order that the Tulica dossier and the report of the investigator be disclosed to the Defence. We shall order that within 14 days, the Defence are to indicate what material in the dossier is not in dispute, what material is in dispute, and the grounds upon which it is disputed. I referred just then to the dossier. I mean to include in that the investigator's report. So the Defence must indicate what's in dispute and what isn't in the dossier and the report, and that should be done by the 2nd of July. We shall then hear, on the 8th of July, the parties in oral argument as to what evidence may be admitted and what witnesses should be called, and the purpose of this order is that the matter should be further clarified for the Trial Chamber to determine the admissibility of the evidence, and the purpose being to expedite the trial, as far as possible, and to concentrate the evidence on those matters which are really in dispute. That order will be put into writing. But meanwhile the parties, having heard it, can act upon it. If, of course, there was any agreement upon these matters between the parties, that would be better still.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I definitely remind you that on the 6th, 7th, and 8th, I will not be here, for what that matters. I have to be elsewhere for the entire week, and on that particular day I have to be at someone's graduation, so I shall definitely not be here. This has very much been my application, and I'm quite happy to leave matters in the hands of others, but if it were otherwise, all the same to the Trial Chamber, and if those days were fully occupied by evidence the following Monday afternoon, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, that will be a day that I will be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll make it the 12th, then, if that's the next sitting day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until the next sitting, which I shall be reminded of. The 6th. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next hearing day is the 6th of July at 2.30. I'm reminded by Judge Bennouna that we have at the moment only one copy of the dossier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There should be more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, three. Does anybody else want to raise anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, (interpretation) in view of the fact that we have moved it from the 8th to the 12th, may we get two days as well? You said until the 2nd of July. Could you allow us until the 4th or 5th of July to submit what we need to submit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The 5th of July.
